Multiply two expressions, retain their constant and linear coefficients, and then repeat the calculation while retaining the quadratic coefficient as well. That extra coefficient can decide whether a change of coordinates exists.

The operation we will study is

With ordinary arithmetic modulo three and , its quadratic interaction can be repaired, but a cubic error remains. If the coefficient is a retained symbol whose square is discarded, the same correction is exact. Keeping its square changes the answer again.

We will calculate each of these cases, then prove the general rule in arithmetic modulo a prime : the operation becomes addition under an invertible coordinate exactly when . Both the coordinate and its inverse will be finite polynomials.

Next, we allow every symmetric operation with zero as its identity, through degree three. We determine every possible coordinate change and the coefficient it cannot remove. A final example passes all the tests through degree eight and fails at degree nine.

Begin with: polynomial multiplication and arithmetic modulo a prime. The rules for retained coefficients are defined explicitly. Equality means equality of coefficients after expansion; no limits or convergence are involved.

This continues How far can a change of coordinates go? The first-order companion uses the same practice of deciding which coefficients to retain.

7 · Keep every possible cubic term

Return to arithmetic modulo three, still allowing explicitly retained coefficient symbols. The quadratic interaction forced a cubic error in . Could a cubic term already present in the operation cancel that error? We now allow both coefficients to vary and calculate which combinations a coordinate change can remove.

For the next three sections, retain all input terms of total degree at most three. Thus

We write for agreement of the retained terms. Each input substituted into an expression has zero constant term, so a discarded term with four input letters can never contribute a term with only three. This is why we can discard it before continuing a calculation.

An expression beginning with always has an inverse as a series, by the recursive coefficient construction in Section 8. That inverse need not stop after finitely many terms. For example, over ordinary numbers modulo cannot have a polynomial inverse: composing it with a nonconstant polynomial of degree gives degree , which cannot be one. The particular pair has the stronger property that both expressions are finite polynomials.

Sources and further reading

The proofs above use the displayed coefficient calculations. These references provide related examples and the wider background.

Henry Shin, How far can a change of coordinates go?, Refactor. The starting example in arithmetic modulo three. The companion Make first order exact develops the practice of retaining specified coefficients. The longer When a Formal Logarithm Fails follows the original coordinate-repair calculation further.

Charles Rezk, Notes on the Hopkins–Miller Theorem, §3.1, printed p. 3, for coordinate changes of addition rules; §3.5, printed pp. 3–4, for the information obtained by repeating an operation times; §5.1–5.3, printed pp. 7–8, for corrections with a square-zero coefficient and the polynomial patterns used in the degree-nine example.

Ariane Mézard, Matthieu Romagny, and Dajano Tossici, Sekiguchi–Suwa theory revisited, Journal de Théorie des Nombres de Bordeaux 26 (2014), 163–200, §2.2, printed p. 167. Background on the family connecting addition with multiplication through a coefficient parameter. The exact repair criterion used here is proved in Section 5.

Jacob Lurie, The Stratification of MFG, Lecture 13, April 27, 2010, printed p. 2, Remark 4. The comparison of leading coefficients after repeating an operation is the general background to the direct calculation in Sections 9–10.
